newsitem.title: JAPAN: JAPAN CAR EXPORTS MAY REKINDLE US TRADE FRICTION.
newsitem.headline: JAPAN CAR EXPORTS MAY REKINDLE US TRADE FRICTION.

text.p: Japanese car exports to the United States rose a steep 75 percent in January from a year ago but industry leaders, worried about possible new trade friction, found nothing to cheer about in the figures.
The Japan Automobile Manufacturers Association (JAMA) said 124,834 units were exported, the fifth straight month of year-on-year gains mainly caused by a weaker yen.
Overall vehicle exports enjoyed a healthy 34 percent growth to nearly 355,200 units during the month, marking the eighth successive month of year-on-year gains in the world market.

The figures were announced only three days after U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright warned on a visit to Tokyo there could be new trade friction if Japan did not keep up its pledge to open its market to American cars.
"January's gain was mainly by Toyota whose exports to the U.S. rose 132 percent," a JAMA official said.
"But looking at those figures, I'm concerned about possible U.S. complaints about the growth in exports," he said.
Toyota said the jump was a one-off event and it expects the growth of its exports to the United States to be flat for the full calendar year.
"The sharply higher exports in January were a passing phenomenon," a Toyota spokesman said.

Toyota's exports to the United States in the next two months would show flat year-on-year growth as the company must focus on domestic sales in the run-up to a planned hike in Japan's sales tax in April, the spokesman said.

Nikko Research senior analyst Noriyuki Matsushima said a general rise in Japanese exports to the United States and increased competitiveness of Japanese cars because of the weaker yen were conspiring to set the scene for trouble.
"Those two factors will reignite trade issues if the U.S. market itself becomes weak," Matsushima said.
He warned that U.S. complaints would be compounded by slow U.S. Big Three car sales in Japan, and slow deregulation of Japan's market for U.S. car parts.

Trade Minister Shinji Sato, already fearful of a trade row, told Japanese auto makers on Tuesday not to exacerbate the situation by lowering the prices of their exports to the United States because of the weak yen.
In a meeting with Sato last Sunday, Albright warned of possible trade friction unless Tokyo fully implemented a 1995 Japan-U.S. auto accord.
Albright said that, since automobiles and auto parts were "key areas," there was a risk of friction developing unless Japan fully implemented the accord.

The American Automobile Manufacturers Association (AAMA) said last month that U.S. car dealerships in Japan numbered 103 at the end of last year, below what the U.S. industry said was its "modest" goal of 200.
Matsushima said the Big Three still needed to do more on their own to improve their competitiveness.
